ai_assessment.comment: A mother on her own cares for three children, one of whom has a physical disability, with no income at all. The recent food assistance and the nearby clinic only partly ease the situation. I recommend inclusion.

explanation.summary: The household should be included: its vulnerability factors are structural and add up, while those pointing towards exclusion are temporary or partial.
rationale: The picture is dominated by three structural elements that do not depend on a one-off event: a mother on her own with three children, no income and a son with a physical disability. Each would matter on its own; together they reinforce each other, because the only adult has to handle childcare, income and her disabled son's appointments by herself.

The two elements that seem to point towards exclusion need to be read carefully. Last month's food distribution was a one-off: it does not change the household's ability to get food in the following weeks, and indeed the family is still skipping meals. The nearby clinic provides access to basic care, but the son's physiotherapy has stopped: having a service nearby is not the same as actually being in its care.

In short, no factor in favour of exclusion offsets, by its nature or its strength, the combination of care burden, lack of income and disability. The rule to remember: temporary support, or a service that is accessible only on paper, is not evidence of stability.

key_points.title: All care falls on one adult
key_points.text: A mother on her own has to look after three children, one with a disability, while also covering basic needs. There is no second adult to share the work or step in when needed.

key_points.title: Food insecurity is ongoing
key_points.text: The household is still skipping meals. Last month's distribution brought relief, but it did not change the household's ability to secure food in the months that followed.

key_points.title: Disability with interrupted care
key_points.text: The clinic is close by, but physiotherapy has stopped. Having a service within reach does not mean the person is actually using it.

key_points.title: No income
key_points.text: With no income and no second adult who could work, the household has no margin to cope with anything unexpected.

pitfalls: Counting recently received assistance as evidence of stability: it is temporary support, not a solution.
Treating the clinic's proximity as guaranteed access to care, without checking that treatment is ongoing.
explanation.ai_note: The AI recommended inclusion. It correctly recognised that the structural factors outweigh the temporary ones.

ai_assessment.comment: A large household displaced for over two and a half years: its size and the length of displacement point to a high risk of vulnerability. The stabilising elements do not appear sufficient to offset this. I recommend inclusion.

explanation.summary: The household should be excluded: it is large and has been displaced for a long time, but it has stable income and housing that cover its basic needs.
rationale: The programme is aimed at households that cannot meet their essential needs on their own. The decisive test is therefore their capacity to cope. Here the household has received stable monthly remittances for over a year, lives in a rented flat with a formal lease, has its documents in order and uses local health services. Taken together, these four elements describe a stable financial and housing situation.

Household size and length of displacement are real factors, but they are indicators of risk, not of current need. They carry weight when they come with concrete shortfalls in food, shelter or care; here no shortfall has been reported. The older dependant is also independent and does not add to the care burden.

The typical mistake, and the one the AI made, is to give a lot of weight to risk indicators and too little to financial stability. Regular remittances are often underestimated because they are hard to capture in the data: that is why a careful reading of the case file is decisive. It is still advisable to schedule a follow-up check in case the remittances stop.

key_points.title: Regular, ongoing remittances
key_points.text: A relative has sent a stable sum every month for over a year. It is a predictable source of income that covers the household's basic needs.

key_points.title: Stable housing
key_points.text: The flat is rented with a formal lease: the household is not living in precarious conditions and is not at risk of losing its home any time soon.

key_points.title: No concrete shortfalls reported
key_points.text: Food, health and safety show no problems. Without a current shortfall, household size and length of displacement remain only indicators of risk.

pitfalls: Being led by household size and length of displacement without checking whether there are current shortfalls.
Assuming the AI opinion is correct: in this case it underestimated the remittances and the stable housing.
Excluding without planning a follow-up check in case the situation changes.
explanation.ai_note: The AI recommended inclusion, with 79% confidence. High confidence does not guarantee a correct opinion: here the model gave too much weight to household size and length of displacement, and too little to remittances and stable housing.

ai_assessment.comment: Single-person household with documents in order. The elements in favour of inclusion and those in favour of exclusion balance out, and confidence in the opinion is low.

explanation.summary: The household should be included: although it is small and its documents are in order, the person is elderly, ill, alone and without a support network.
rationale: Single-person households are often seen as a lower priority because they have fewer needs “in quantity”. Here, though, what matters is the nature of the need. A 74-year-old woman with a chronic illness and reduced mobility, alone and without a network, cannot collect goods on her own, access care regularly or ask for help in an emergency.

Having her documents in order and her registration completed is positive, but it concerns formal access to services, not the practical ability to use them. With no one to accompany or support her, formal access does not turn into actual assistance. For the same reason the short length of displacement is not reassuring: need depends on her fragility, not on how much time has passed.

This case was marked as complicated precisely because the standard indicators point in opposite directions. When that happens, the automated opinion is not reliable and the caseworker's careful reading of the file is the only thing to rely on. The criterion to apply is whether the person can meet her basic needs without help, and here she cannot.

key_points.title: Social isolation

key_points.title: Dependence on assistance

pitfalls: Treating a small household as a synonym for lower need.
Taking documents in order as a guarantee of actual access to services.
Underestimating the complicated-case label: it calls for a careful reading of the whole file, not a quick decision.
